<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                <jats:p>In Mozambique, infection by intestinal parasites is reported all over the country. However, infection in children with diarrhoea is mostly focused in the southern region of Mozambique. This work aims to determine the frequency and potential risk factors for infection by <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp., <jats:italic>Giardia lamblia,</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>Entamoeba histolytica</jats:italic> in children under-five years hospitalized with diarrhoea in <jats:italic>Hospital Central de Nampula</jats:italic>, northern Mozambique.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                <jats:p>A cross-sectional hospital-based surveillance was conducted between March 2015 and January 2018 in children admitted with diarrhoea in <jats:italic>Hospital Central de Nampula</jats:italic>. Sociodemographic information was obtained through semi-structured interviews applied to the children’s caregivers. A single stool sample was collected from each child to detect antigens from <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp., <jats:italic>G. lamblia,</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>E. histolytica</jats:italic> using an immune-enzymatic technique. Crude and adjusted odds ratios (with 95% Confidence Intervals) were obtained by logistic regression models to identify factors associated with infection by <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp. and <jats:italic>G. lamblia</jats:italic>.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                <jats:p>The median age and interquartile intervals of our sample population was 12 months (8–20). Intestinal protozoa were detected in 21.4% (59/276). <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp. was the most common protozoa (13.9% - 38/274), followed by <jats:italic>G. lamblia</jats:italic> (9.1% - 25/274) and <jats:italic>E. histolytica</jats:italic> (0.4% - 1/275). Children with illiterate caregiver’s (<jats:italic>p</jats:italic>-value = 0.042) and undernourished (<jats:italic>p</jats:italic>-value = 0.011) were more likely to be infected by <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp. <jats:italic>G. lamblia</jats:italic> was more common in children living in households with more than four members (p-value = 0.039). <jats:italic>E. histolytica</jats:italic> was detected in an eleven month’s child, co-infected with <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp. and undernourished.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec><jats:sec>
                <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                <jats:p><jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp. and <jats:italic>Giardia lamblia</jats:italic> were the most common pathogenic intestinal protozoa detected in children with diarrhoea hospitalized in the <jats:italic>Hospital Central de Nampula</jats:italic>. Our findings obtained highlight the importance of exploring the caregiver’s education level, children’s nutritional status for infections with <jats:italic>Cryptosporidium</jats:italic> spp., and living conditions, namely crowded households for infections with <jats:italic>G. lamblia</jats:italic> in children younger than five years.</jats:p>
              </jats:sec>
title: Intestinal protozoa in hospitalized under-five children with diarrhoea in Nampula – a cross-sectional analysis in a low-income setting in northern Mozambique

assertion.value: The ViNaDia protocol was approved by the Mozambique National Committee for Bioethics in Mozambique (IRB00002657, reference Nr. 348/CNBS/13). Written informed consent was obtained from caregivers, after explaining the ViNaDia aims and procedures. Data confidentiality was ensured by storing the physical data collection and consent forms in a lockable cabinet with access only to the ViNaDia investigators.
